sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
July 2026 delivered a deeply bifurcated global equity tape defined by two countervailing forces: a geopolitical shock from resumed U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian infrastructure that sent Brent crude from under **$70/bbl** to an intra-month peak near **$105/bbl** on July 23, and a final-session surge driven by Amazon's historic Q2 earnings print. The S&P 500 ended essentially flat at **7,489.72** (**-0.1%**), the Nasdaq Composite shed **-3.2%** to **25,373.85** — its worst monthly performance since late 2025 — while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained **+0.4%** to **52,485.03**, recording its fourth consecutive monthly advance as energy and value names led the tape.

European indices delivered the month's strongest performance among major regions: the DAX surged approximately **+4.8%** (approx., verify before merging) to close near **25,800**, ending July near a record high driven by energy sector outperformance and resilient industrial earnings. The FTSE 100 gained approximately **+3.0%** (approx., verify before merging) to close near **10,674** (approx., verify before merging), while the CAC 40 advanced a more modest **+0.9%** (approx., verify before merging). Within APAC, performance was starkly divergent: Japan's Nikkei 225 fell **-8.1%** to **64,362** from its June 30 close of **70,062** as BOJ hawkish signals and a technology sector rout weighed heavily, and the Shanghai Composite declined **-6.4%** to **3,832.26** from its June 30 close of **4,094.40** on tariff and property sector headwinds. The APAC standout was the Hang Seng, which surged approximately **+13.1%** (approx., verify before merging) to **25,884** from a depressed June 30 close of **22,881**, propelled overwhelmingly by the energy sector boom in Hong Kong-listed oil majors.

The month's defining dynamic was the radical re-pricing of geopolitical risk premiums. The divergence between a resilient Dow — buoyed by energy, industrials, and financials — and a declining Nasdaq encapsulates an equity market in genuine regime transition: from a narrow, AI-concentration-driven advance toward a cross-asset repricing that rewards energy, value, and shorter-duration cash flows over speculative technology multiples.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes:
US-Iran War Escalation & the Crude Oil Supply Shock -- The single most consequential market event of July 2026 was the resumption of U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear and energy infrastructure, reversing the ceasefire-driven normalization that had briefly sent Brent to **$69/bbl** on July 2 following June's peace memorandum. Brent surged to an intra-month peak near **$105/bbl** on July 23 as tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — a conduit for approximately a fifth of global oil and LNG — was halted for multiple days, and Iraq cut output by roughly 1.5 million barrels per day due to storage limits and blocked exports. By July 31, Brent settled near **$92/bbl** (approx., verify before merging) as U.S. naval escorts provided partial mitigation, posting its best monthly performance in over two years.

The oil supply shock delivered an immediate stagflationary impulse to an economy already navigating elevated Federal Reserve vigilance. Airlines, chemical producers, and logistics companies — many of which had rapidly reduced crude hedges on June's ceasefire news — faced severe near-term margin compression with minimal buffer, and sell-side analysts began revising Q3 2026 earnings guidance downward across energy-intensive sectors. Energy sector equities globally registered their strongest monthly performance in years, with U.S. E&P names and European and Hong Kong-listed integrated oil majors posting double-digit monthly gains.

For financial markets, the re-escalation materially complicated the H2 2026 macro narrative. The Hormuz route remains partially disrupted, and any further deterioration in U.S.-Iran negotiations could push Brent back toward or above **$100/bbl** — a threshold that would almost certainly force a Federal Reserve policy response and trigger a more abrupt de-rating of equity multiples. The episode underscores how fragile the June peace dividend proved to be and how quickly structural supply constraints can reassert themselves in a geopolitically fractured world.

Amazon Blowout & the Big Tech Q2 Earnings Season -- Amazon's July 30 Q2 2026 results delivered one of the most consequential single-stock earnings reports in recent memory: worldwide net sales of **$200.6 billion** — the company's first quarter exceeding the **$200 billion** threshold — up **+20%** year-over-year and ahead of the **$196.62 billion** consensus estimate. AWS cloud revenue grew **+37%** year-over-year to **$42.2 billion**, the fastest growth rate in 18 quarters, as AI inference workloads and enterprise cloud migrations drove demand materially above expectations. GAAP earnings per share came in at **$5.75**, heavily boosted by a **$53.4 billion** gain on Amazon's Anthropic investment, while operating income climbed to **$27.5 billion** from **$19.2 billion** in Q2 2025.

Amazon's beat headlined a broadly constructive earnings season for U.S. mega-cap technology: Microsoft, Meta Platforms, and Apple also reported Q2 figures ahead of consensus, with S&P 500 operating earnings growth for Q2 2026 tracking approximately **+15%** (approx., verify before merging) year-over-year. The Amazon-driven surge on July 31 lifted the S&P 500 more than **+1%** on the final trading day, effectively rescuing the index from a materially deeper monthly drawdown and enabling the Dow to post its fourth consecutive monthly gain.

However, the market's reaction to the earnings season was notably muted relative to the magnitude of the beats. Amazon guided full-year 2026 capital expenditure to **$220 billion** — roughly **+50%** above 2025 levels — contributing to a collective hyperscaler AI infrastructure commitment estimated above **$500 billion** across the four major cloud operators. Investors are increasingly pricing a scenario where AI infrastructure investment will not generate commensurate revenue returns for multiple quarters — a concern that contributed directly to Nasdaq's **-3.2%** monthly underperformance despite historically strong underlying profit growth.

Federal Reserve's Divided Hold and September Hike Risk -- The Federal Reserve's July 28-29 FOMC meeting produced no policy change — the committee voted 9-3 to hold the federal funds rate at **3.50%–3.75%** — but the unprecedented three-dissenter split, with Cleveland's Hammack, Minneapolis's Kashkari, and Dallas's Logan each voting for an immediate **+25 basis point** hike, signaled a materially hawkish shift in the committee's center of gravity. Chair Kevin Warsh, in his second press conference since assuming the chair, stated the Fed "will deliver price stability" and "will not hesitate to act," removing any residual forward-guidance language suggesting a neutral policy stance. CME FedWatch subsequently priced a greater-than-**50%** probability of a rate hike at the September 2026 FOMC meeting.

U.S. Treasury yields reacted immediately: the 10-year note finished July at **4.75%**, while the 2-year yield settled at **4.28%**, resulting in a 10-2 spread of **+47 basis points** as the curve modestly steepened. The 30-year Treasury yield reached its highest level since 2007 (approx., verify before merging specific level), reflecting the combined weight of AI-driven corporate debt issuance, ongoing sovereign supply, persistent fiscal deficit concerns, and energy-driven long-term inflation risk. Rate-sensitive sectors including REITs, utilities, and consumer staples underperformed the broader index materially on a monthly basis.

For asset allocators, the prospect of a hiking cycle resumption in September 2026 — barely one quarter after the prior tightening impulse had been absorbed — introduces the risk of a more aggressive trajectory than consensus had assumed entering H2. The Fed's central dilemma remains unchanged: an energy-driven supply shock is inherently stagflationary, punishing real growth while simultaneously demanding a policy response that further tightens financial conditions. How Chair Warsh navigates this trade-off will be the defining macroeconomic question for the remainder of 2026.

Section 338 Tariff Escalation After Supreme Court Ruling -- The Trump administration's trade policy underwent a critical structural shift in July as new tariffs took effect under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, the administration's legislative response after the Supreme Court ruled that the prior year's reciprocal tariffs imposed under emergency trade authorities were unlawful. The resulting framework places most trading partners under tariff rates of **10%** to **12.5%**, with significantly higher rates on select categories — including a **50%** tariff on certain Canadian goods — creating visible supply-chain disruption signals across manufacturing PMI surveys globally. The complex and overlapping tariff structure drove an uptick in corporate guidance withdrawals as compliance teams at multinationals struggled to operationalize the framework in time for Q3 planning.

China bore the sharpest immediate cross-asset impact beyond oil: the Shanghai Composite fell **-6.4%** to **3,832.26**, pressured by trade restrictions, below-consensus economic data, and continued property sector deleveraging. The Caixin Manufacturing PMI export orders sub-index contracted for a second consecutive month, validating the earnings-risk narrative for China-exposed multinationals. Crucially, Hong Kong-listed equities behaved very differently from mainland Chinese names — the Hang Seng surged approximately **+13.1%** (approx., verify before merging), driven by energy sector outperformance from CNOOC, PetroChina, and Sinopec, which benefit directly from Brent moving from **$69/bbl** to near **$92/bbl**.

For global portfolio managers, the tariff framework's new legal foundation under Section 338 is structurally significant: unlike the voided reciprocal measures, this basis may prove more durable to judicial challenge, establishing a potentially longer-lived trade policy environment. Several major investment banks downgraded their China A-share outlooks to underweight during July, citing the combination of tariff uncertainty, property sector overhang, and reduced domestic policy space, while selectively upgrading commodity-exposed names in Hong Kong given the energy sector tailwind.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
U.S. equity performance in July 2026 was defined by an increasingly stark divergence between value-oriented large-caps and growth-heavy technology names. The Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced **+0.4%** to close at **52,485.03**, driven by energy sector leadership — major E&P and integrated oil names each gained double digits on the crude surge — alongside financial sector resilience and healthcare stability. The S&P 500 ended essentially flat at **7,489.72** (**-0.1%**), masking significant cross-sectional dispersion; equal-weight S&P 500 outperformed the cap-weight version materially as energy and industrials dominated while mega-cap technology weighed on aggregate index returns.

The Nasdaq Composite bore the heaviest losses, declining **-3.2%** to **25,373.85** — its worst monthly performance since late 2025 — as a wave of de-risking in long-duration growth names preceded and initially overshadowed the Q2 earnings season. Concerns centered on AI capital expenditure sustainability: the collective 2026 capex guidance from Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Meta exceeded **$500 billion**, raising fundamental questions about whether infrastructure investment at this scale could be justified by near-term AI revenue returns. Philadelphia Semiconductor Index names were particularly volatile around critical TSMC and Nvidia guidance updates.

The decisive turning point came on July 31 when Amazon's Q2 2026 blowout — **$200.6 billion** in revenue and AWS growth of **+37%** — catalyzed a broad market rally that lifted the S&P 500 more than **+1%** on the final trading day, rescuing the index from a materially deeper monthly drawdown. The month's outcome — a fourth consecutive winning month for the Dow, Nasdaq's worst month in over a year, and a flat S&P 500 despite extraordinary intra-month volatility — is the clearest signal yet that equity leadership is rotating away from the mega-cap growth complex toward value, energy, and dividend-yielding sectors.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equity markets were the standout regional outperformers in July 2026, with energy sector strength and resilient industrial earnings driving among the best monthly returns of any major equity region globally. The DAX surged approximately **+4.8%** (approx., verify before merging) to close near **25,800**, ending the month near a record high as integrated energy names and machinery exporters benefited directly from the crude surge. The FTSE 100 advanced approximately **+3.0%** (approx., verify before merging) to close near **10,674** (approx., verify before merging), while the CAC 40 posted a more modest **+0.9%** (approx., verify before merging) gain as the index's relatively lower energy weighting and higher consumer sector exposure produced a more muted outcome.

The re-escalation of U.S.-Iran hostilities proved a structural tailwind for European large-cap indices given their significantly heavier energy sector weighting relative to U.S. benchmarks. BP, Shell, TotalEnergies, and ENI collectively gained double-digit percentages in July, accounting for a disproportionate share of regional outperformance. European industrials also benefited from continued defense spending momentum as NATO member nations accelerated procurement in response to fresh geopolitical instability, providing incremental revenue tailwinds for Airbus, Rheinmetall, and BAE Systems.

Not all European sectors benefited equally: automotive stocks declined on U.S. tariff uncertainty, with German OEMs particularly exposed to the new Section 338 framework. European banks were mixed — the prospective September Fed rate hike provided a net interest margin tailwind for cross-border operations, but higher oil-driven inflation raised concerns about consumer loan quality in Southern Europe. The European Central Bank maintained its policy rate unchanged at its July meeting, noting it would monitor energy price pass-through before adjusting its own path, preserving rate-differential dynamics that partially supported EUR/USD.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asia-Pacific equity markets delivered a strongly divergent performance in July 2026, with the region's three major bourses moving in markedly different directions under distinct but intersecting macro pressures. Japan's Nikkei 225 fell **-8.1%** to close at **64,362** from its June 30 close of **70,062**, as the Bank of Japan's increasingly hawkish signals on potential rate normalization strengthened the yen and compressed the export-earnings multiple that had underpinned the index's exceptional year-to-date advance. A rout in Korean and Japanese semiconductor and electronics names, intersecting with BOJ policy uncertainty, added a further layer of pressure that the final-day global rally could not fully offset.

The month's APAC standout was the Hang Seng Index, which surged approximately **+13.1%** (approx., verify before merging) from its June 30 close of **22,881** to **25,884** on July 31. The outsized gain was driven overwhelmingly by Hong Kong-listed energy majors — CNOOC, PetroChina, and Sinopec — whose equity valuations rerate sharply when Brent crude moves from **$69/bbl** to **$92/bbl** over the course of a single month. The Hang Seng's recovery also reflected bottom-fishing after the index had severely underperformed global peers through the first half of 2026 on China macro concerns, with the index entering July near its lowest YTD levels.

Mainland China was the clear regional laggard. The Shanghai Composite fell **-6.4%** to **3,832.26** from its June 30 close of **4,094.40**, pressured by U.S. Section 338 tariff escalation, below-consensus Q2 GDP data, and continued property sector deleveraging. The PBOC cut the reserve requirement ratio for select banks mid-month but refrained from broader stimulus, disappointing markets pricing more aggressive easing. The contrast between the Hang Seng's energy-driven rally and Shanghai's tariff-driven decline encapsulates the increasingly bifurcated nature of the China investment thesis, where Hong Kong-listed commodity names and Shanghai-listed domestic demand names are subject to fundamentally different earnings drivers.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
Currency markets in July 2026 were shaped by the interaction of three competing forces: geopolitical risk-driven safe-haven demand for the U.S. dollar, the inflationary impulse of higher crude oil prices, and growing expectations of a September Fed rate hike. The DXY traded in a range of approximately **98.84** to **102.68** (approx., verify before merging) during the month, settling near **100** (approx., verify before merging) at July month-end as the immediate Strait of Hormuz risk premium partially faded and the Fed's July statement provided no additional catalyst to break the recent trading range. The range-bound outcome reflects competing pulls of dollar safe-haven demand during geopolitical spikes against the structural headwind from a historically elevated U.S. current account deficit.

EUR/USD held near **1.14** (approx., verify before merging) at month-end, as the euro benefited from energy sector terms-of-trade improvement in European current accounts while the ECB's July hold limited rate-differential widening. GBP/USD traded near **1.33** (approx., verify before merging), with sterling supported by resilient UK labor market data and the Bank of England's continued hold. The most significant developed-market FX move was in the Japanese yen: USD/JPY approached **161** (approx., verify before merging) as BOJ hawkish signals proved insufficient to drive sustained yen appreciation against a dollar still supported by higher U.S. real yields, while crowded yen carry-trade positioning remained vulnerable to any further BOJ language shifts.

Emerging market currencies experienced broad-based pressure in July as Section 338 tariff escalation triggered capital outflows from EM assets. The Chinese yuan's controlled but persistent depreciation reflects official tolerance for a weaker exchange rate as a partial offset to export volume losses. EM central banks in commodity-importing economies faced a particularly acute policy trade-off: defending currencies against a weak domestic growth backdrop while import inflation from higher energy prices eroded real household purchasing power — a constraint that limits their ability to ease policy in response to slowing growth.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
July 2026 was defined almost entirely by crude oil and the geopolitical events that drove it. Brent crude commenced July near **$69/bbl** — reflecting the June peace memorandum between the U.S. and Iran — before surging to an intra-month peak near **$105/bbl** on July 23 as U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian infrastructure triggered tanker traffic halts through the Strait of Hormuz and Iraqi production cuts of approximately 1.5 million barrels per day. By July 31, Brent settled near **$92/bbl** (approx., verify before merging), representing a monthly gain of approximately **+28%** (approx., verify before merging) from the June 30 close — its best monthly performance in over two years. WTI crude tracked comparable moves, closing near **$88/bbl** (approx., verify before merging) at month-end.

Gold ended July near **$4,043/oz** (approx., verify before merging), essentially flat for the month, as safe-haven demand from geopolitical tensions was offset by the competing headwind of rising real Treasury yields. With 10-year TIPS yields moving above **2.3%** (approx., verify before merging), the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding gold remains elevated relative to recent history. Copper gained in July to near **$6.49/lb** (approx., verify before merging), supported by AI data center construction demand driving electrical wire and transformer requirements, alongside supply disruptions from South American mining regions that tightened physical market balances.

For corporate earnings, the crude oil move has two distinct second-order effects: it represents a material earnings acceleration for energy producers globally, while simultaneously imposing margin compression on airlines, shipping companies, chemical producers, and consumer goods manufacturers that will crystallize in Q3 2026 guidance. The EIA and IEA revised their H2 2026 global oil demand forecasts upward, assuming sustained Hormuz supply disruption will require strategic petroleum reserve releases by consuming nations to partially compensate — a dynamic that limits the ceiling on any near-term oil price correction.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
U.S. Treasury yields moved meaningfully higher in July as oil-driven inflation expectations and rising September rate-hike probability combined to push the curve upward across tenors. The 10-year Treasury note finished July at **4.75%**, while the 2-year yield settled at **4.28%** — resulting in a 10-2 spread of **+47 basis points** as the curve modestly steepened. The 30-year Treasury yield reached its highest level since 2007 (approx., verify before merging specific level), reflecting the combined weight of AI-driven corporate debt issuance, ongoing sovereign supply, persistent fiscal deficit concerns, and energy-driven long-term inflation risk pushing the long end materially higher.

The Federal Reserve's 9-3 vote to hold at **3.50%–3.75%** — with Hammack, Kashkari, and Logan dissenting in favor of an immediate **+25 basis point** hike — and Chair Warsh's explicit price stability commitment shifted terminal rate expectations materially. Fed funds futures ended July pricing a greater-than-**50%** probability of a hike at the September 2026 FOMC meeting, a dramatic reversal from rate-cut expectations prevailing in prior months. This repricing drove a meaningful widening in 30-year mortgage rates, further dampening the housing market recovery that had begun in Q1 2026.

Credit markets showed early signs of stress: investment grade corporate spreads widened by approximately **+15 basis points** (approx., verify before merging) and high yield by approximately **+40 basis points** (approx., verify before merging) over the course of the month, as energy-driven inflation and rate-hike risk combined to pressure leveraged balance sheets and increase refinancing risk for lower-rated issuers. European sovereign spreads — particularly Italian BTPs — widened modestly on oil price inflation pass-through concerns, while UK Gilts tracked Treasuries higher in yield. For fixed income allocators, the July repricing suggests a regime where neither the short nor the long end provides a clear safe harbor, and active duration management will be a key performance differentiator through H2 2026.
